jury.summary_md:

Unsure: the B16 breach and the 1.9 ha cut off the 1:3,000 site plan come from my own overlay on the site data, not from the panels. Noise protection can't be confirmed, because the entry's noise model leaves out the railway. The 150 kV strip can't be checked. Sealing differs between panel 2 (39.6 % + 2.5 %) and the text (33.8 % + 15.3 %). Whether a Special Mention is too lenient is the jury's own call. No closed-competition material was seen.

narrative.summary_md:
Two Banks, *A district that faces its loudest line*: the railway and Pilsen-Allee are treated as the river of Regensburg North, with work facing the line from both banks, homes on the slopes between seven tributaries and the centre on the Station Bridge. Second run written: `text.md` (the brief's eight points, 3 to 4 sentences each, then how it was approached, where it moved from the idea, the sealing statement and homes and residents per phase; about 1,770 words for the 3 to 4 A4 pages, pp. 12, 34), `communication.md` (785 of 800 signs, p. 12), and `measure_design.py`/`.json`, which check the finished massing against the principles.
Key number: 6 crossings of the line, the longest gap 389 m against 724 m today (`narrative/measure_design.json`; the structure plan gives 395 m). Also measured: 0 homes, schools or daycares on land at 65 dB(A) or more, and 0 m² of building on the 4.49 ha air corridor.
Least sure, and where the design moved from the framework: the bank row is closed along 47 % (west) and 38 % (east) of the line against the 70 % target; 430 homes sit above the work on the banks; the market hall stands beside the deck, not on it, and the deck is drawn 16 m plus a 4 m path, not 30 m; both landmarks are on the west head; sealing is 49.1 % by `analysis` and 42.1 % by `open-space/sealing.csv`, both over the 40 % target (the text uses analysis); only 55 % of the home footprint keeps to the air axis; walking reach to the stop is 52 % (structure plan) or 5 % (mobility), so it is left out of the text. # Analysis

Reads: site-kit, brief-reader
Reads (end): massing, every analysis, drawing-graphics

Measure, never guess. Use only the project's site folder (`site.geojson` and its layers) and the brief's `checklist.md`, opened at the brief's pages it names; for the second run add `massing/massing.geojson`. Never write a site, a place or a number of this project into the skill or a script. Every value carries its source (layer, brief page) or is named as an assumption, and a layer or destination the data lacks is left out and named in `summary.md`. Work in Python, in a metric projection, inside the site polygon only (`pip install -r requirements.txt`: shapely, pyproj, networkx).

**What it measures.** Each measure is one row per value in `metrics.csv` and one map.
- **Uses:** the area and share of the site per land use, from the plots and buildings.
- **Edges:** what the site boundary meets (street, rail, water, built, open land), its length in metres, and how many street or path crossings each stretch has.
- **Green:** the green land and its share, split into wooded, open green and farmland, and the brief's green per resident, if the brief gives residents.
- **Walking reach:** the share of the site within 400 m and 800 m along the street and path network of each destination the data has: stations, green, shops and schools. A destination the data lacks is named in the summary as missing and is not measured.
- **Sealed share:** fully sealed (buildings, streets), partly sealed (paths, squares, pitches) and unsealed, in hectares and as a percentage of the site. The class of each land use goes in `config.json`, marked as an assumption.
- **What to keep:** `keep.geojson`, with the existing buildings inside the site, water, woods, scrub, nature reserves and everything the checklist says must stay that the layers show. Each feature has a `reason` and a `source` (the brief's page). Whatever the checklist names but the layers lack goes in the summary.

**Start from the scripts.** Copy `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/config.example.json` to `analysis/config.json` and fill it from the checklist, each value with its page. Then run `python "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/measure.py" --proposal <proposal folder> --site <site folder> --config <proposal folder>/analysis/config.json --state today` and `draw.py` with the same arguments. On the second run, `--state design` measures the massing in place of what it covers inside the site, with the same method. Then `compare.py --proposal <proposal folder>` reads every `metrics.csv` in the proposal folder and writes `comparison.csv` (`measure, unit, today, design, change, better`) and `comparison.md`, which says in a few lines where the design improves on today and where it doesn't. Whether higher or lower is better comes from `config.json`.

**What to write.** Everything into `analysis/`: `config.json`, `metrics.csv` (`measure, value, unit, state, source`, with `state` either `today` or `design`), `keep.geojson`, a map per measure as SVG with a PNG next to it, the comparison on the second run, and `summary.md` in three lines: what you measured, the sealed share, and what you are unsure of. The maps take their look from `drawing-graphics/standard.md` if it exists, else black lines on white with greys. Open the maps once before you finish.

# Brief reader

Reads: pdf-to-md

The checklist belongs to the brief, not to one version, so it is written once and reused. If `checklist.md` lies next to the brief's Markdown in the project's `brief/` and is newer than every Markdown there, copy it into `brief-reader/` in the proposal folder you are told, write `summary.md`, and stop.

Otherwise read the brief's Markdown in parts, never all at once: list its headings and page markers (`<!-- page N -->`) with `grep`, then read the pages that hold the task, the programme, the rules, the submission and the jury's criteria. Write `checklist.md` next to the brief, in this order, one line per item, each ending with its source as `(<file> p. N)`:

- `## Numbers`: homes, residents, areas per use, green per resident, phases, and every other figure the design must meet.
- `## Rules`: heights, setbacks, what must stay, what is not wanted.
- `## Drawings and scales`: every drawing asked for, with its scale.
- `## Panels and format`: how many panels, their size and orientation, the texts and their length.
- `## Required content`: a numbered list of every item the brief requires on the panels or in the text, in the brief's words.
- `## What the jury looks for`: the criteria, as the brief states them.
- `## Pages`: each topic above and the pages to open for it, so other skills read only those.

Copy it into `brief-reader/` in the proposal folder. Never invent: what the brief doesn't say is written as "not stated". `summary.md`: three lines, the size of the task in one sentence, the number of required items, and what the brief leaves unclear.

# Narrative

Reads: brief-reader, analysis, climate
Reads (end): everything
Model: opus

This skill runs twice: first it builds the conceptual framework the project grows from, then it writes the text that explains the finished project. Work in the proposal folder you are given and write only into `narrative/`. Read the brief's checklist (`brief-reader/checklist.md`), `analysis/` and `climate/`; if one is missing, use the brief's Markdown and the site folder, and say so in `summary.md`. Never invent a fact: every claim names its file and, where there is one, the brief's page. Everything about the competition and the place comes from the brief.

**First run: the framework.** It must be memorable and solve a conflict, and it may be bold and abstract. Answer from the brief and the analysis what the project is for, who will use it and what it should say. Draft three stories in words, each with a different character (the site, its users or an abstract theme): its desire, the conflict in its way, and the transformation the design brings. Where no character comes naturally, use concept, angle and object. Choose the strongest, check that it doesn't restate the brief's own plan if the brief shows one, and add a move of your own that can be drawn and counted. The other skills design from this, so keep it clear. Write `narrative.md`:

- **Story:** the three answers, the three drafts in one sentence each, the chosen one and why, and its character, desire, conflict and transformation.
- **Title and subtitle:** short and memorable, not a slogan; the subtitle at most about eight words.
- **Idea:** one clear sentence without jargon, a paragraph on why this site asks for it, and your own move.
- **Principles:** three to five, one line each, that the design skills can check (where green runs, how dense, how people move). A principle may set its own target, marked as one.
- **Storyline:** one section per panel, in the number and format the checklist gives: its message in one line, and the drawings that carry it, named by the existing skills that make them.
- **Jury:** each criterion from the checklist and where the storyline answers it, or "open" or "partly open".

**Second run: the text.** Read every `summary.md` and table in the proposal folder. Write `text.md` for the jury, explaining the finished project in sequence: the idea, the concept, how it was built up (structure, programme, buildings, open space, movement, phases) and how it was approached (what the site showed, what was decided and why). Fit it into the brief's headings, length and language where the brief sets them, and put any other text it asks for, such as a short one for publication, in a file of its own. Give each key figure its source file in a footnote, and leave out figures that don't exist. Leave `narrative.md` as it is: the drawings were made from it. If the design has moved away from the framework, tell it in `text.md` and name the gap in `summary.md`.

**After each run**, write `summary.md` in three lines: the title and the idea in one sentence; the number that matters most to the idea, with its source; what you are least sure of.

# Programme

Reads: brief-reader

1. Read the brief checklist written by `brief-reader` in the proposal folder you are told, else the newest one. If it is missing, read the brief's Markdown in the project's `brief/`; if a figure is in neither, ask or say so in `summary.md`.
2. Take from the brief everything it asks to build, and table it:
   - **Homes and households:** the number of homes or the housing floor area, the household mix and unit types, and the residents. Where the brief gives a total but no mix, say so and leave the mix open; never invent shares.
   - **Uses and their areas:** commerce and ground-floor uses, schools and daycares with their capacity and outdoor space, community and sport, and anything else the brief lists, each with its gross floor area and plot.
   - **Shared and productive space:** uses shared by day and night, gardens and urban agriculture, shared amenities, only where the brief asks for them or gives a number.
3. Never invent data: next to every number, its source in the brief (with its page) or the assumption behind it, such as m² per resident. No drawings; text and tables only.
4. Write everything into `programme/` in the proposal folder and nothing outside it:
   - `programme.csv`: `use, area_m2, plot_m2, homes, residents, source`, one row per use, so `massing` can check its floor area against it.
   - `households.csv`: `household, share, homes, source`, if the brief gives a mix.
   - `programme.md`: what the brief asks for in words, and its open questions.
5. Create a `summary.md` of exactly three lines:
   - What you tabled.
   - The one key number that matters (total homes).
   - The one assumption or uncertainty you're highlighting.

# Structure plan

Reads: narrative, climate, programme
Model: opus

Set the urban figure in `structure-plan/` of the proposal folder: neighbourhoods, centres, green, routes and gateways, nothing finer. Take the idea and its numbers from `narrative/`, the corridors from `climate/`, homes per phase and commerce from `programme/` (else the brief), the site from the site folder; name what is missing in `summary.md`. Use `site.geojson` as it is and only report where it disagrees with the brief.

**Design.** Start from what is there: keep, then change, then new. Open gateways where streets, stops and landscape meet the site, and continue them in. Name neighbourhoods by their spatial qualities, never by assumed residents. Put the main centre on the stop and gather the homes around it; local centres take the rest. Give green real extent and roles, and keep climate corridors free. Keep homes out of the climate's loud zones and put commerce there to shield them. Follow the narrative's figure and numbers exactly (how many islands on which side, a width, a distance), or say why the site forbids it.

**Hold the programme.** Each phase holds its homes and its floor area (homes, commerce) under the storey cap with 15 % to spare; where it falls short, enlarge the neighbourhoods before raising density. At least half of the homes lie within a 400 m walk of the stop, or say why not.

**Build.** Copy `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/design.example.py` to `structure-plan/design.py`: one `F.programme(...)`, then one `F.add(...)` per feature, decisions only. Run `python "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/build.py" <proposal>/structure-plan/design.py --site <site> --proposal <proposal> --climate <climate>` and change `design.py` until `checks.txt` shows no SHORT, in at most four builds. They also warn when the first phase has less of the land than of the homes, a main or local route runs over a kept building or along a foot way, or a water green lies above the ground around it. The scripts check every field, clip to the site, cut routes out of neighbourhoods and measure every area. `scripts/georef.py` places a picture from the brief on the site. Needs `pip install shapely pyproj`.

Features: `neighbourhood` (`phase`, `homes`, `density`, `commerce_m2`), `centre` (`level` main or local, `holds`: the stop, shops, a school), `green` (`roles`), `route` (`level` main, local or landscape) and `gateway`, each with `action` (keep, change, new), `basis` (documented, brief, mapped, hypothesis) and `source`.

**`summary.md`, three lines:** the figure, with the homes and floor area each phase holds against those asked; the share of homes within a 400 m walk of the stop, from `checks.txt`; the hypothesis that matters most and the evidence that would settle it. Write nothing else.

# Art direction

Reads: every drawings (end)
Model: opus

Work in the proposal folder you are given, else the newest in the project's `proposals/`; write only to its `art-direction/`. You judge; you never draw or change another skill's files. Read the summary of each drawing skill, the standard in `drawing-graphics/`, and the project's reference images (where its `CLAUDE.md` says, else `references/`) with the file there that says which images are of which kind. If the proposal folder has side-by-side sheets in `.compare/` (references left, ours right, at one print size), look at each once; else open each drawing's PNG beside the references of its kind. Without references, compare with the standard alone and say so in `summary.md`.

For each drawing, find the largest differences from its references, the ones you see first from across the room: what is drawn and what is left out, the amount of detail, the weight of the figure against the ground, the hierarchy, the labels, how the drawing fills its frame. Turn the largest into at most three fixes per skill, each one its scripts can carry out and you could check, saying what to change and by how much ("draw the street trees as crowns at every scale", "label each centre with its uses, as the references do", "crop to the new district and 100 m around it"), never "make it richer". A fix asks only for what a design layer, the narrative or the standard gives, never for invented data. A gap in colour, line weight or font belongs to the standard: name it in `notes.md`, not as a fix. Never copy a reference's text, title or name. A skill whose drawings already come close gets no fixes.

Write `art-direction/fixes.json` as `{"<skill>": ["fix", ...]}`, only for skills that drew something, `{}` when none needs a fix. Write `notes.md`: per drawing, the references you compared it with and the differences, largest first. End with `summary.md` in three lines: how many fixes for how many skills; the largest gap; what you're unsure of.

# Jury

Reads: brief-reader, panel-layout (end), narrative (end)
Model: opus

Work in the proposal folder you are given, else the newest in the project's `proposals/`; write only to its `jury/`. Read every panel as an image, the plans up close, then `narrative/`, the checklist in `brief-reader/` and the brief (where the project's `CLAUDE.md` says, else `brief/`). With no panels, say so in `summary.md` and give no verdict. Judge only what the entry shows and the brief says, and never look up results or other entries. The project's reference images (where its `CLAUDE.md` says, else `references/`) are inputs: compare the drawings with them, drawing by drawing, and say where the entry falls short. Trust the drawing over the caption: what the text promises and the plan doesn't show is missing. Recompute the entry's numbers against the brief's exact requirement, compare its figure and boundary with the brief's plans, and cite a panel or brief page for each claim.

Write `report.md` in the brief's language, as a Swiss jury report cut down to one entry, in the jury's sober voice ("is missed", "is questioned", "fails to fully convince"), with no contents page, member list, thanks or signatures:

1. **Task and criteria:** the task briefly, then the brief's criteria. They are rarely weighted, so the jury weights them itself before judging and says why, as carrying, contributing or supplementary, never in percentages. Weights the brief gives apply.
2. **Preliminary check:** without judgement, in tables: formal requirements, required contents, material requirements. Then the jury decides on admission; gaps don't exclude automatically.
3. **Rounds:** hurdles, following the brief's procedure where it has one, because one entry can't be compared. Say which it passes, where it is eliminated and why, and end with a control round that tests bringing it back.
4. **Appraisal:** continuous prose. Start with the siting, name strengths before doubts, give the key figures a paragraph, end on one or two overall sentences.
5. **Verdict:** in the brief's award levels, with no ranking.
6. **Recommendations for further work:** a list of tasks, also for an eliminated entry.

Unless the brief weights its criteria otherwise, test every entry hardest on its interior: how its buildings work inside or, at a larger scale, how its blocks and uses are organised. Where the panels don't show it, say so. Where open space is the idea, a plan that doesn't show it still counts against the concept. Also judge the unwritten criteria: self-evidence, fit with the place, and whether a political majority could back it. Mark these as assessments, supported by the entry and the brief. End with `summary.md` in three lines: the verdict and round; the number that weighed most; what you're unsure of.

# Panel layout

Reads: brief-reader, narrative, structure-plan
Reads (end): everything
Model: opus

Work in the proposal folder you are given, else the newest in the project's `proposals/`, else a new `proposals/<YYYY-MM-DD>_draft/`, never the project's top folder; write only to its `panel-layout/`. Needs Python 3.11+ and Chrome, Edge or Chromium (no other installs). First run `python "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/panels.py" scan <proposal folder>`: it lists every summary, drawing (with its print size and the scale its skill gives), table and text, and the inputs that are missing. Read every `summary.md`, the storyline and title from `narrative/`, and the format from `brief-reader/checklist.md`. If there is no checklist, read the format from the brief itself (where the project's `CLAUDE.md` says, else `brief/`): panel size and count, orientation, file limit, reserved boxes such as a code field, panel numbers, names and titles that must appear, the drawings and figures it asks for, and its language. Read the whole brief for these, not only its general submission rules: a site's own list of drawings, scales and figures often comes later, in the task or an appendix. Cite the PDF page for each, not the printed page number. The look comes from `drawing-graphics/standard.md`: fonts, colours, line weights. Without it, leave `style` out: the script's default is black on white with one accent colour. Never pick a look of your own.

**First run, before the drawings: plan the panels.** Each panel has one hero drawing across its full width (the site plan, a detail area or a close isometric), with bands above or below it: the thematic plans (such as mobility, open space, climate, phases) in frames of one size at one scale, the long section across the width, a large frame for the isometric close up. If the project has reference images of whole panels (where its `CLAUDE.md` says, else `references/`), look at each once and compose as they do: how they split into bands, how large the main drawing is, where the title and the numbers sit; never take their titles, texts or names. For every drawing the brief requires and the storyline needs, write an item in `layout.json` with the `file` its skill will write, its `scale` and its `frame` in mm, and in `shows` what it must show; list each in `required` (a storyline drawing with `"source": "storyline"`) with its `file` and, in `by`, the skill the project's list of skills says makes it (leave `by` out if unsure); give the required drawings their frames first, and size each frame at its scale from the extent of what it shows in the structure plan (the new district, a centre), else of the site. Render once: a drawing not made yet prints as a grey labelled frame. Look at the panels as a whole, move frames until they read well, save `layout.json` also as `layout-plan.json`, which no later run changes, and end with `summary.md`. The drawing skills then draw to their frames.

**Second run, with the drawings.** Open the first run's `panel-layout/layout.json` and fill it in as `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/layout.md` describes: don't read the brief again or rebuild its format, reserved boxes, marks, `required` or frames (`layout-plan.json` keeps them; the report names every planned item not placed and every change to a planned drawing). Run `python "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/panels.py" render <proposal folder>/panel-layout/layout.json --check` (no browser) until its report shows nothing you can fix, then once without `--check`. One panel per step of the storyline; without a storyline, the order the brief lists its drawings in, from the large scale to the small. A plan from `plans/` is the one that goes on a panel; a check plan of the same thing from `massing/` never does. A drawing with a scale goes in a frame at a true scale, never stretched: where the brief fixes its scale, it keeps that scale and the frame crops it; where the brief gives none, set `"scale": "auto"` and the script picks the scale, then crops. Where the brief asks for a graphic scale, set `"scale_bars": "all"` in `format`. Aim the crop at what the brief asks to show. The report names a required drawing whose frame hides more than 25 % and a drawing drawn at another scale than the one fixed: ask its skill to draw it to its frame, never shrink it. Never drop a planned drawing: if it doesn't fit its frame, take the next usual scale where the brief allows it, else resize or move its neighbours. Leave reserved boxes empty. Each panel says a few things large rather than everything small. No text is smaller than 12 px (9 pt) printed, and no line of text runs wider than about 65 characters: a wide text box is set in columns. The script holds both; don't work around them. Every number on a panel shows its source; take the numbers from the tables and summaries, never make one up. The few the storyline rests on go on as big type (`"type": "number"`), each with its source in one line, not as rows of a table. If two numbers that should agree don't (such as a total and the sum of its phases), the panel shows the number of the skill that designs that thing (the homes per phase of the skill that plans the phases, the sealed share of the skill that lays out the open space), with its source; put the other in `notes` and `summary.md` with the mismatch, and never correct either; the report names `figures` rows with one label and two values until `notes` does. Text belongs to `narrative`: use its words, shortened if needed, not your own.

Read `panel-layout/report.md` and look at every `panel-N.png`. Fix what doesn't fit, what overflows and what overlaps. A drawing that never came stays as its empty frame. Every drawing `issues.md` names as available but not on the panels goes on one, at its scale, unless it still doesn't fit after its neighbours move. A number or statement the brief asks for goes on as a `figures` box or a `number`, from the tables that hold it, with their sources. Before a panel is done, fill space left with drawings from the folder that the storyline can use; never blow up a diagram or add content of your own to fill it. Check again with `--check`; render in full at most three more times. What the brief asks for and nobody made stays listed as missing in the report: don't draw it yourself. `issues.md` is the studio lead's list of what other skills must fix, by skill; fix everything under "Fix in panel-layout" yourself. End with `summary.md` in three lines: the panels made and what they show; the one number that matters (how many of the brief's required items are on the panels); what you're unsure of, and how many issues `issues.md` hands to other skills.

# Ground floor

Reads: brief-reader, massing, programme, structure-plan, mobility, open-space, streets

The massing gives every new building its `ground_floor` use and owns it; this skill adds what a detail plan needs on the ground, by rules, never placed by hand. Take the brief's numbers (bus bays or platforms at a hub, bike spaces, play areas) from its checklist, and the brief only at the pages it names; never write a place or a number into the skill. Never change another skill's file: a use refined here (a food market put into a shop floor at a centre) is written into this skill's file only, and a change the massing should make goes in `summary.md`.

Work in the proposal folder you are told, else the newest in the project's `proposals/`, and write only into `ground-floor/`. Copy `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/config.example.json` to `ground-floor/config.json` and fill it, each value with its page or the reason for an assumption: `centre_uses`, the uses with an area that the programme and the structure plan's `holds` put into a centre's ground floors; `hubs`, the bus bays and bike spaces the brief asks for at a hub of `mobility/` or a centre; the bike stands per door and a courtyard's play area. Then run `python "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/ground_floor.py" --proposal <proposal folder> --config <proposal>/ground-floor/config.json` (`pip install shapely pyproj`, no Rhino). This skill converts each PDF with Docling, which keeps headings, lists and tables in reading order, so a number in a table stays next to its label. A marker `<!-- page N -->` stands before each page, so whoever takes a number from it can cite the file and the page.

Convert the PDFs the user names, or else every PDF in the project that has no Markdown yet. Write each result next to its PDF, so every version of a proposal reads the same text. For each: `python "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/pdf_to_md.py" <pdf> <the PDF's folder>/ --images`. Add `--ocr` only if a page comes out empty but has text in the PDF, a scan. It writes `<name>.md` and the pictures (maps, plans, drawings, photos) at 300 dpi to `<name>-images/`, named by page, leaving out icons and logos under 3 cm. Plans and maps drawn in vectors also go to `<name>-drawings/` with the legend beside them, as PDF, SVG and PNG (`pip install pymupdf`). The first run downloads Docling's models, about 500 MB. If Docling isn't installed: `pip install docling`.

Then read each result against its PDF on a few pages with tables or key numbers. Fix nothing by hand. Next to each, write `<name>-summary.md`, one page at most, from its Markdown: what the document is and from whom, then what matters most in it (the task, key numbers and areas, dates, what it requires), each line with its page `(p. N)`. Only what it says; add nothing. Keep an `index.md` in the same folder, one line per PDF: where it came from, what it is, its pages. Write `summary.md` next to it, in three lines: which PDFs were converted, how many pages and tables, and any page that came out wrong or empty.
